title: Digestive Biscuits
subtitle: semi-sweet wholemeal biscuits for eating and baking
excerpt: Homemade digestive biscuits are far better than the commercial version -- more buttery, more wholemeal, with a proper crumbly snap. They are worth making for eating alone and for use in cheesecake bases and other recipes that call for crushed digestives.
sourceNotes: The digestive biscuit was first developed in Scotland in the 1830s. The name is misleading -- they have no particular digestive property.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in a tin lined with baking paper. Defrost at room temperature.
recipe.batchNotes: Double easily. Keeps for 2 weeks in an airtight tin.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough keeps in the fridge for 3 days before baking.

content.text: The dough will feel dry and crumbly -- this is correct for a digestive. Press it together firmly rather than adding more liquid. Roll it between two sheets of baking paper rather than on a floured surface; it is much easier to handle this way.

items.prepNote: use 100g wholemeal flour and 50g plain flour

content.text: Combine both flours, brown sugar, baking powder, and salt. Rub in the cold butter until the mixture resembles fine breadcrumbs.
Add the cold milk and bring together into a stiff dough. It will be dry. Press it together firmly -- do not add more liquid. Flatten into a disc, wrap, and chill for 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 180C. Roll the dough between two sheets of baking paper to about 3mm thick. Cut into 7cm rounds.
Place on lined baking sheets. Prick each biscuit all over with a fork. Bake for 12 to 15 minutes until golden at the edges.
Leave to cool on the tray for 5 minutes before moving to a rack. They will firm and crisp as they cool.

items.cause: Too dry, or butter not rubbed in finely enough.
items.fix: Rub the butter in until there are no visible lumps. Add the milk and press the dough hard with your hands -- it will come together.

items.cause: Not baked long enough, or not cooled on the hot tray.
items.fix: Digestives harden as they cool. Leave them on the tray for 5 minutes. If still soft, return to the oven for 3 minutes.

content.text: The digestive biscuit is the most eaten biscuit in Britain. It is the foundation of cheesecake bases, a vehicle for tea-dunking, and a stand-alone snack eaten by virtually everyone. The commercial version has been largely unchanged since the 1890s. The homemade version has a better butter flavour and a more satisfying crumble.
